scenes.title: The Tally Desk
scenes.text:
The bell at the Salt Exchange rang six times before the light came over the flats, and by the sixth stroke Ilse Marrow had her sleeves pinned back and her pen cut and the day's first ledger open on the slope of the tally desk.

She liked this hour. The great hall was empty except for the porters sweeping out yesterday's grit, and the windows along the east wall were still grey, and the only sound was the brooms and, under them, the long breath of the tide going out across the mud. In an hour the hall would be full of factors shouting prices and lightermen shouting back and the clerks of the six houses arguing over whose scales were honest. For now it was hers.

The ledger was the lading book for the *Constant*, a coaster out of Harl that had come in on the evening tide with forty-two hundredweight of white salt in sacks. Ilse ran her finger down the column. Forty-two sacks, each a hundredweight, each stamped with the Harl mark. Received at the north quay by the weigher, a man named Pell whose sevens looked like ones. Carried by lighter to the Exchange cellars. Entered.

She turned the page to the cellar book, where the same salt should have been entered again by the cellarman, and frowned.

Forty-six.

She checked the date, checked the mark, checked that she had not turned two pages at once. Forty-six sacks of Harl white, received into cellar three on the night of the ninth. Four more than had come off the ship.

"Morning, Miss Marrow."

She did not jump, though it was a near thing. Merrit Vael stood at the end of the desk with his hat in his hand. He was the master of the guild, a tall, soft-spoken man with grey in his beard and ink on his cuffs like any clerk, and he had a way of arriving in a room without having walked into it.

"Master Vael. You're early."

"So are you. So are you always, I'm told." He nodded at the open book. "The *Constant*?"

"Yes, sir."

"Anything wanting?"

She could have said no. Afterwards she would wonder why she didn't, and the only answer she could find was that she had been a tally clerk for six years and her whole worth in the world was that she said what the numbers said.

"The cellar book has four more sacks than the lading book. Forty-six against forty-two."

Vael came around the end of the desk and looked. He looked for a long time, long enough that she could hear the porters' brooms again.

"Pell," he said at last. "Pell writes his sixes like his twos. I've told him." He tapped the lading entry with one finger. "That's a forty-six, Miss Marrow. Look at the tail on it."

She looked. It was a two. She had seen Pell's twos a thousand times and this was one of them, and the tail on it was the tail on all his twos, a little hook like a fishing barb.

"I'll check with the ship's master," she said.

"The *Constant* sailed on the morning ebb." Vael closed the ledger, gently, the way you'd close a book someone had fallen asleep over. "Write it up as forty-six. I'll have a word with Pell about his hand."

"Sir."

He smiled at her and put his hat on and went out through the side door, and Ilse sat looking at the closed cover for a while. Then she opened it again and copied both entries, the lading and the cellar, onto a scrap of tally paper, and folded the scrap twice, and put it inside her stays where it lay against her ribs all day like a cold coin.

By seven the hall was full. Factors from the inland houses stood under the great clock with their samples in little linen bags and tasted salt off the backs of their hands. A Harl agent argued with a Varrow weigher about moisture. Somebody's dog got in and was chased out. Ilse entered the *Grace of Tidings* and the *Meg* and a lighter-load of grey salt from the south pans that was mostly sand, and did not think about the *Constant* more than once an hour.

At noon Sefa came by with bread.

Sefa was apprenticed to a dyer in Weld Street and her hands were blue to the wrist and would be, she said, until she died, and probably after. She sat on the step below the tally desk, which was not allowed, and tore the loaf in half.

"You've got your counting face on," she said.

"I always have my counting face on. I count."

"Your other counting face. The one where something doesn't add." Sefa chewed. "Is it a man?"

"It's four sacks of salt."

"Oh," said Sefa. "Well, that's much worse."

Ilse almost told her. She had the words in her mouth. But Master Vael crossed the far end of the hall just then, talking with a woman in a grey council cloak, and he glanced up at the tally desk, and Ilse swallowed the words with the bread.

"Tobin's in tonight," she said instead. "He's bringing the *Gull* round from the south pans. Come and eat with us."

"Can't. Mistress Orley's got a vat of woad going and she says if it isn't stirred on the hour it'll go green, and if it goes green she'll have my hide for a dye bag." Sefa stood and brushed the crumbs off. "Tell your brother he still owes me a shilling."

"He'll say he paid it."

"He'll be lying," said Sefa, and went.

scenes.title: The North Quay
scenes.text:
The fog came in with the evening tide, as it did most nights in the last month of the year, rolling over the flats in a low white wall that swallowed the marker poles one by one. By the time Ilse reached the north quay the far end of it was gone, and the lamps on the lighters moored along the wall were only smudges, and the water slapping against the stones sounded close and secretive, like someone talking in the next room.

Tobin was sitting on a bollard with his back to her, smoking.

"You'll catch your death," she said.

"Catching it's easy. It's keeping it I can never manage." He did not turn around. "You're late."

"I had a ship from Harl and a dispute about sand." She sat on the next bollard. The stone was wet through her skirt. "You're early. I thought the *Gull* was coming round on the tide."

"She did. I brought her round on the last of the flood and got her in before the fog." He nodded down at the water, where the lighter lay against the wall, black and squat, with her single mast unstepped and lashed along the deck. "Empty now. We offloaded at the south cellars."

Something in the way he said it made her look at him. Tobin was two years younger than she was, and broader, and he had their father's face, which meant that he could not hide anything at all and had never once in his life managed to. In the lamplight his face was grey.

"What's wrong?"

"Nothing's wrong."

"Tobin."

He drew on the pipe and let the smoke go into the fog, where it was lost at once. "There was a man on the south pans. Waiting when we came in. He wanted to know if we'd take a load across to the Exchange tonight instead of in the morning. Paid in advance. Silver, not scrip."

"That's not wrong. That's lucky."

"He wanted it brought to the river door," said Tobin. "Not the quay. The river door, under the cellars. At the bottom of the tide."

Ilse said nothing. The river door was an old water gate under the Exchange, from the days when the salt barges came down the Varrow instead of across the flats. It had been bricked up when she was a child. She had walked past the brick of it a hundred times.

"The river door's closed," she said.

"That's what I told him. He said it wasn't." Tobin turned the pipe over and knocked it against the bollard. "He said four sacks. He said no one would weigh them and no one would ask."

The scrap of tally paper inside her stays seemed to grow colder.

"What did you say?"

"I said I'd think about it." He looked at her for the first time. "I said no, Ilse. I'm not a fool. I said no, and he said that was a pity, and that the *Gull* was a fine old boat and it would be a shame if anything happened to her at the bar. And then he walked off into the fog, and Dall and I unloaded, and I came here to wait for you."

"Who was he?"

"I don't know. Not a pans man. Not a Varrow man, I'd say. He had a southern way of talking, soft at the ends." Tobin shrugged. "He had a ring. A seal ring, with a ship on it. That's all I saw."

Ilse took the scrap of paper out of her stays. It was warm now, and a little damp, and she unfolded it and held it so the lamplight fell on the two numbers.

"There were four extra sacks of Harl white in cellar three this morning," she said. "Four that didn't come off the ship."

Tobin read it. He read slowly; he always had. Then he folded it and gave it back.

"Then someone's already doing it," he said. "And they wanted me to do it next."

"Master Vael said it was Pell's handwriting."

"Is it?"

"No."

They sat on the bollards while the fog thickened and the lamps on the lighters went out one by one as the lightermen turned in. Somewhere down toward the bar a bell buoy rang, slow and lopsided, the way it did when the tide was turning.

"Don't tell anyone," said Tobin.

"I wasn't going to."

"I mean it. Not Sefa, not your clerk friends, not that old woman in the archive. If somebody's walking salt in through a bricked-up door under the Exchange, it isn't Pell and it isn't some southern man with a ring. It's somebody with a key."

"There's no key to a brick wall."

"Then somebody with a trowel," said Tobin, "and the say-so to use it." He stood up and stretched, and the bollard creaked as his weight came off it. "Come on. I've got a fish and you've got a fire, and if we don't eat soon I'll start on the rope."

She walked with him back along the quay, past the dark lighters, to the stair that went up to Coil Lane and the two rooms over the chandler's where they had lived since their mother died. At the top of the stair she looked back. The fog had closed right over the quay now. She could not see the *Gull* at all, only the place where her lamp had been.

scenes.title: Fire on the Water
scenes.text:
Somebody was hammering on the door.

Ilse came up out of sleep the way you come up out of cold water, all at once and gasping. The room was dark. The fire was a red eye in the grate. Tobin's cot across the room was empty, the blanket thrown back.

"Ilse! Ilse, open the door!"

Sefa. She knew the voice before she knew she was standing, and she had the bar off the door and Sefa was in the room, still in her dye apron, her hair coming down, her blue hands grabbing at Ilse's arms.

"It's the *Gull*," Sefa said. "She's burning. She's out on the bar and she's burning. I saw it from the roof at Orley's, I was up stirring the vat, I saw the light—"

"Tobin's here." Ilse turned to the cot as if he would be in it. "He was here. We ate. He went to bed."

"Then where is he?"

They ran. Down the stair, along Coil Lane, down the second stair to the quay, where the fog had thinned to rags and there were people already, lightermen in their shirts, a woman with a baby wrapped in a shawl, two boys from the rope walk. Everyone was looking the same way, out across the black water toward the bar, where a long orange smear of fire lay on the dark like a wound.

"That's the *Gull*," said one of the lightermen. "That's Marrow's boat."

"Who took her out?" Ilse's voice came out high and strange. "Who took her out? She was empty. She was moored right there."

The place where the *Gull* had been moored was empty water. The painter was gone from the ring.

"Saw her go out on the ebb, an hour back," said the lighterman, a heavy man named Coby whom Ilse knew a little. "Thought it was your brother. Didn't think anything of it. Lot of the lads go out to the bar on the ebb to fish the channel."

"In the fog?"

Coby shrugged, and did not look at her.

Out on the bar the fire leaned over and went down, slowly, the way a candle goes when it falls into its own wax. Then there was only a red glow on the water, and then nothing at all, and the bell buoy ringing.

"Get a boat," Ilse said. "Somebody get a boat out. He might be in the water."

Nobody moved. It was Sefa who said it, gently, her blue hand on Ilse's back.

"Ilse. It's slack water at the bar. If he's in it, he's—"

"Don't."

"—he's swimming. Tobin swims like a seal. You know he does."

Two of the lightermen were already unshipping oars. A boat went out, and then another, their lanterns swinging. Ilse stood at the edge of the quay and watched them go into the dark. She found that she had the scrap of tally paper in her hand, though she did not remember taking it out. She had slept with it under her pillow.

The boats were gone an hour. When they came back, the first held three men and a coil of burnt rope. The second held Tobin.

He was sitting up in the stern, soaked to the skin and black with soot, his left hand wrapped in somebody's shirt. He was alive. Ilse's knees went, and Sefa held her up, and for a moment the whole quay swam.

Then she saw the two men in the boat behind him, in the dark blue coats of the harbour watch, and the way one of them had his hand on Tobin's collar.

scenes.title: The Watch House
scenes.text:
The harbour watch kept its house at the foot of Tarrant Stair, a squat stone building with barred windows that had been a customs post in the old days and still had the king's arms over the door, half worn away by salt. Inside it smelled of tallow and wet wool. There was a long bench, a table, a fire, and at the back an iron door with a grille.

Tobin was behind the iron door.

"He's not under arrest," said Captain Orrin. "Not yet. He's under my eye. There's a difference, and I'd advise you to be grateful for it."

Dace Orrin was younger than Ilse had expected for a captain of the watch, perhaps thirty, with a long serious face and a scar through one eyebrow that gave him a look of permanent mild surprise. He had taken off his coat and was writing in a daybook at the table, and he did not stop writing while he talked to her.

"He was in his bed," Ilse said. "He went to bed at ten. I heard him."

"Did you hear him get up?"

"No. I was asleep."

"Then you heard him go to bed and you didn't hear him get up, and an hour after midnight his boat was seen going out on the ebb, and an hour after that it was burning on the bar, and he was in the water beside it." Orrin dipped his pen. "Miss Marrow, I'm not saying he set it. I'm saying I've a burnt lighter across the main channel at the bottom of the tide and every ship due in on the morning flood will have to stand off until we clear it, and the owner of the lighter was the only man found in the water."

"It's his boat. Why would he burn his own boat?"

"Insurance," said Orrin, without looking up. "Debt. A woman. A quarrel with his partner. I've seen men burn their boats for all of those, and once for a dog." He wrote something. "What's the matter with his hand?"

"I don't know. He was hurt. He was hurt getting her off, or putting the fire out, I don't know."

"He says he woke and the boat was gone and he went down to the quay and saw her going out, and took a skiff after her, and when he got to her she was already burning and there was nobody aboard. He says he burnt his hand on the tiller trying to bring her round." Orrin looked up at last. "Does that sound like your brother?"

It did. It sounded exactly like Tobin. It was the most Tobin thing she had ever heard.

"Yes."

"It sounds like a story to me," said Orrin. "But I've been wrong." He closed the daybook. "Go home, Miss Marrow. He'll be here in the morning. The magistrate sits on Thursday."

"That's three days."

"It's two. Today's Tuesday." He stood, and she saw that he was tired, and that the hand he put out to take his coat off the chair was not steady either. "If there's anything you know about how that boat got out to the bar, now is the time to tell me. Not Thursday. Now."

She thought of the southern man with the ring. She thought of the river door, bricked up, and the four sacks of Harl white, and Master Vael closing the ledger gently, like a book someone had fallen asleep over. She thought of Tobin saying *don't tell anyone*.

"No," she said. "Nothing."

Orrin looked at her for a moment longer than was comfortable. Then he nodded, as though she had told him something after all, and opened the street door for her.

Outside, Sefa was waiting on the step, her apron wrapped round her shoulders against the cold. The fog had gone. The sky over the flats was black and pricked with stars, and the tide was coming back in, filling the channels with a sound like a long slow pour of sand.

"Well?" said Sefa.

"Thursday. The magistrate sits on Thursday."

"Then we've got until Thursday." Sefa put her arm through Ilse's and started walking her up Tarrant Stair. "What do you need?"

Ilse stopped on the stair.

"Sefa," she said. "What were you doing on the roof at Orley's at one in the morning?"

"Stirring the vat. I told you. It goes green."

"The vat's in the yard. Not on the roof."

Sefa looked at her, and then laughed, a short tired laugh with not much in it.

"There's a man," she said. "He's a ropemaker. We go up on the roof. It's the only place Mistress Orley can't hear the door. Is that what you want to know?"

"I'm sorry."

"Don't be. He's not much of a man. He talks about hemp." Sefa tugged her on up the stair. "But I saw what I saw, Ilse. I saw the boat go out. There was a light on her when she went out, a little light at the stern, like a lantern. And there was somebody at the tiller. I couldn't see who. But they were steering. Somebody was steering her out to the bar."

"Before she burned."

"Before she burned."

scenes.title: A Page from Cellar Three
scenes.text:
She did not go home. She went to the Exchange.

It was not yet four. The night porter, an old man named Gedd who had known her father, let her in by the side door without a question, because she had a key to the tally room and was often in before dawn, and because, she thought later, he had heard about the *Gull* and was too kind to mention it.

The cellar books were kept in the tally room in a cupboard with a lock. She had a key to that, too. She lit a lamp and took down the book for cellar three and opened it to the ninth.

Forty-six sacks of Harl white. The same hand, the cellarman's careful round hand. She turned back a week and found another entry, a coaster called the *Pelican* out of Cray: thirty sacks lading, thirty-three in cellar. Back another fortnight: the *Wren*, fifty and fifty-five.

She sat down on the floor of the tally room with the book in her lap and turned pages until the lamp began to gutter. It went back to midsummer. Every week, sometimes twice in a week, a ship came in with a lading of white salt, and the cellar book took in a few sacks more than the ship had brought. Never many. Three, four, five. Never from the grey salt or the pan salt, which nobody wanted except for curing. Always the white.

At midsummer it stopped. Before midsummer the books matched, sack for sack, as far back as she cared to look.

Ilse took out her penknife.

She had never in her life defaced a ledger. In six years she had never so much as blotted one. Her father had been a tally clerk and his father before him, and the one thing they had both told her, the one thing that she had believed the way other people believed in the gods of the tide, was that a ledger was a promise: that whatever else was false in the world, the book was true, because a clerk had made it so.

She cut the page for the ninth out of the cellar book, close to the binding, the way you'd take out a page that had been spoiled with ink. She folded it with the scrap of tally paper and put them both inside her stays. Then she put the book back in the cupboard and locked it and blew out the lamp and sat in the dark until the six o'clock bell.

When the porters came in to sweep, she was at the tally desk with her sleeves pinned back and her pen cut, as she always was.

scenes.title: Hanne
scenes.text:
The archive of the Salt Exchange was below the waterline, which everyone agreed was a terrible place to keep paper and which nobody had ever done anything about. You went down a stair behind the cellars, and down another, and along a passage where the walls sweated and the lamps had to be kept in glass, and at the end there was a door with a brass plate that said RECORDS in letters so worn you could only read them with your fingers.

Hanne Sallow had kept the archive for forty years. She was small and bent and wore three shawls at once, and she had a little brazier going at all hours that she said was for the damp and that Ilse suspected was mostly for her feet.

"The Marrow girl," Hanne said, without looking up from the book she was mending. "I heard about the boat. Sit down. Don't touch anything."

Ilse sat on the only other stool. The archive was a long low room with a vaulted ceiling, and shelves ran the whole length of it, floor to ceiling, packed with ledgers in leather and ledgers in board and ledgers in nothing at all, held together with string. At the far end the shelves disappeared into a darkness that the lamps did not reach. Somewhere in that darkness water was dripping, slowly and steadily, as it had dripped, Hanne said, since before the Exchange was built.

"I need to see the plans," Ilse said. "The old plans of the building. From when the river gate was open."

Hanne stopped sewing.

"Why?"

"Because somebody's using it."

Hanne put down the needle and looked at her properly for the first time, over the top of a pair of spectacles that were mended at the bridge with wire.

"Your father," she said, "used to come down here and sit on that stool and ask me questions he oughtn't. He never once told me why. You've a better manner than he had." She got up, all three shawls rustling, and took the lamp. "Come on, then. Mind the floor, it's slick by the third bay."

The plans were in a flat chest at the back of the room, under a tarpaulin, in a drawer that stuck. Hanne pulled it with both hands and it came out in a gust of mould. Inside, between sheets of yellowed tissue, were drawings of the Exchange as it had been a hundred years ago, before the flats were drained, when the river still came down past the north wall and barges unloaded straight into the cellars.

"There," said Hanne. She put a finger on the drawing. "The water gate. Here's your cellars, one through six. Here's the gate, under cellar three. There was a ramp up from the river, and a slip, and a winch for the sacks."

"Cellar three," said Ilse.

"That mean something to you?"

"It might."

Hanne grunted. "When the river was turned they bricked the gate and filled the slip with rubble. But the culvert's still there. It has to be. The cellars would flood every spring tide if the water had nowhere to go." She traced a line on the drawing with her fingernail, a thin double line that ran from under cellar three out across the edge of the sheet. "Runs out under the old town. Comes up, if I remember, in the drowned warehouses on the east flats. Nobody's been down it in my lifetime. Rats, maybe."

"Could a man walk it?"

"A small man. At the bottom of a spring tide. If he didn't mind rats." Hanne looked at her sideways. "Or a woman."

Ilse looked at the drawing for a long time. The ink had faded to brown, and the culvert was only a faint ghost of a line, but it was there, and it went where Hanne said.

"Can I take this?"

"No."

"Can I copy it?"

"You can sit here and copy it with my pen and my ink and then you can put it back in the drawer and close it, and if anybody ever asks me, you came down to look at the lading books for your father's year, which you've done before, and I gave you a lamp and went back to my mending." Hanne lowered herself onto a stool by the chest. "And then you can tell me why the master of the guild came down here three days ago and asked to see the very same drawing."

Ilse's pen stopped.

"Master Vael?"

"Who else is master of the guild? He came on Saturday afternoon. He looked at it for half an hour and asked me where the culvert came out and I told him what I've told you. He was very civil. He's always very civil." Hanne pulled her shawls tighter. "He didn't ask to copy it. I suppose he didn't need to."

"Did he say why?"

"He said the council was considering whether to open the gate again, for the spring tides. Drainage. Councillor Brennick's notion. He said she'd asked him to look into it." Hanne shrugged. "It's possible. They've been talking about the spring tides for years. Every year the water comes a little higher."

Ilse finished the copy without saying anything. When it was done she rolled it inside her sleeve, and Hanne put the drawing back between its tissues and shut the drawer, which took both of them, and then they stood together in the lamplight among the shelves.

"Your brother," said Hanne. "Is he a fool?"

"Sometimes."

"Is he a liar?"

"No. He can't. He's got our father's face."

"Then you'd better be quick," said Hanne. "Because Gerrit Pell, who weighs on the north quay, came down here yesterday to ask me if the archive kept copies of the cellar books, and I told him we did, and he went away looking like a man who'd swallowed a hook." She sat back down to her mending. "He's frightened. Frightened men talk. Go and find him before somebody else does."

scenes.title: The Rope Walk
scenes.text:
She did not find Pell. Pell, the north quay foreman told her, had not come in that morning, nor sent word, and his wife had been round twice asking for him. The foreman was not worried. Pell drank, he said, and when he drank he sometimes slept in the sail lofts.

Ilse looked in the sail lofts. Pell was not there. She went back to the Exchange and did a day's tally with her copy of the culvert in her sleeve and the page from cellar three against her ribs, and she did not make a single mistake, which she was afterwards rather proud of.

It was dark when she came out. The streets of the old town were narrow and crooked and the lamps were few, and she had walked them all her life and knew every step, which is why she knew, by the bottom of Weld Street, that she was being followed.

She did what her father had taught her. She did not hurry. She did not look round. She turned into the rope walk, which was a long covered alley three hundred yards long where the ropemakers twisted hemp in the daytime, and which at night was empty and dark and smelled of tar. Halfway down there was a place where the roof had fallen in and you could step out of the walk into the yard of a cooper's. She stepped out, and waited behind a stack of staves, and counted.

At thirty, a figure came past the gap in the roof. It stopped. It looked into the cooper's yard.

"You're very good," it said. "But you breathe like a bellows."

It was a woman. She was young, younger than Ilse, with cropped black hair and a sailor's coat too big for her, and she stood in the gap with her hands in her pockets as though she had all the time in the world.

"Who are you?"

"Kesh." The woman came into the yard and sat down on an upturned barrel. "Just Kesh. You're the Marrow girl. Tally clerk. Sister of the man who burned his boat."

"He didn't burn it."

"I know he didn't. I watched who did." Kesh smiled. She had a gap between her front teeth. "That's what I've come to sell you."

Ilse came out from behind the staves.

"Sell."

"I'm a woman of business. Everybody in Varrow is. You count salt, I carry things." Kesh took a hand out of her pocket and turned it palm up. "Five crowns."

"I haven't got five crowns."

"Then you can't afford what I know." Kesh shrugged and began to stand.

"Wait." Ilse put her hand to her sleeve, where the copy of the culvert was. "I can't pay you. But I can tell you something you don't know."

Kesh sat back down.

"There's a culvert," said Ilse, "under the Exchange. It runs from the old water gate out to the drowned warehouses on the east flats. Somebody's using it to bring white salt into cellar three that never went through the scales. Three or four sacks a time, since midsummer. And the master of the guild went and looked at the plans of it on Saturday."

Kesh was quiet for a while. Somewhere out in the old town a dog was barking, and a woman was shouting at the dog, and the dog was not listening.

"That's worth something," Kesh said at last. "That's worth something to the right people. All right, Marrow. Here's mine for yours. The man who took your brother's boat out was a southerner. Big, soft-spoken, wears a seal ring. I've carried for him, once or twice. He calls himself Corran. That's not his name."

"How do you know?"

"Because I've seen his real name," said Kesh. "On a letter. In a place I'm not going to tell you about tonight." She stood and pulled the big coat around her. "Spring tide's on Thursday. Bottom of the ebb is two hours before dawn. If you want to see where your culvert comes out, meet me at the end of the east causeway on Wednesday night, and wear boots you don't love."

"Thursday's when the magistrate sits."

"Then you'll want to be back by breakfast," said Kesh, and went out through the gap in the roof, and was gone.

scenes.title: Coil Lane
scenes.text:
Captain Orrin was sitting on the stair outside her door when she got home.

He had a lantern beside him on the step and his hat on his knee, and he stood when he saw her, which no one from the watch had ever done for her before.

"Miss Marrow. I've been waiting an hour. Your neighbour the chandler thinks I've come to arrest you, and has been very kind to me in consequence. I've had two cups of his tea." He picked up the lantern. "May I come in? It won't take long."

She let him in. The room was cold and she knelt and made up the fire while he stood in the middle of the floor with his hat and looked at everything — Tobin's cot, the table, the shelf of their father's ledgers, the oilskin hanging on the door — in the slow, even way of a man adding a column.

"Your brother owes money," he said. "To a man named Ferris, on the south pans. Eleven crowns. Did you know?"

She had not known. She kept her back to him and fed the fire a stick at a time.

"He owes it for the *Gull*'s new mast, I think," Orrin went on. "Which is now at the bottom of the main channel. It's the sort of thing a magistrate likes to hear, Miss Marrow. A debt, and a boat, and a fire. He'll think he's heard the whole story in the first five minutes, and he'll stop listening."

"Then why are you telling me?"

"Because I don't think it is the whole story." He set the lantern on the table. "Gerrit Pell is missing. Did you know that?"

"I heard. I looked for him."

"So I'm told. You looked in the sail lofts, and the foreman's office, and the Lantern, and at his house. You were quite thorough." He turned his hat round in his hands. "So was somebody else. A man came to Pell's house this morning, before you. Big man, his wife says. Polite. Asked for her husband and left a coin for the children." He paused. "She said he had a ring."

Ilse stood up. The fire had caught and she could feel it on the backs of her legs.

"What sort of ring?"

"She didn't say. Do you know what sort?"

For a moment she nearly told him. The scrap of tally paper and the page from cellar three were both against her ribs, and the copy of the culvert was in her sleeve, and it would have been the easiest thing in the world to take them out and put them on the table under his lantern and say *here, you add it*. He had a good face for it. He had stood up when she came along the landing.

But Tobin had said *somebody with a key*, and Orrin had a key to the cell her brother was sitting in.

"No," she said.

Orrin nodded slowly. He did not look surprised, or angry; he looked, if anything, a little sad, the way her father used to look when a column came out wrong for the second time.

"You said that to me last night, too," he said. "In the same voice." He put his hat on. "When you're ready to tell me, Miss Marrow, I'll be at the foot of Tarrant Stair. I'm always there. It's the curse of the job."

He went out. She heard him go down the stair, and the chandler's door open, and the chandler say something hopeful, and Orrin say something short. Then it was quiet.

She sat down at the table where his lantern had been and took a fresh book off the shelf — one of her father's, never used, with a marbled cover — and cut her pen, and began to write down everything that had happened since six o'clock on Monday morning, in order, with the times as near as she could put them. She did not know why. It was what she knew how to do.

She wrote until the fire went down, and then she went to bed, and did not sleep.

scenes.title: The Causeway
scenes.text:
The east causeway ran out from the end of Gull Street onto the flats for half a mile and then simply stopped, as if whoever had built it had looked at the mud ahead and lost heart. Beyond it there was nothing but the dark and the smell of the sea and, very far off, the low black shapes of the drowned warehouses, which had been the warehouses of the old river port before the river was turned, and which now stood up to their knees in mud and up to their shoulders in water twice a day.

Ilse was there at midnight in her father's sea boots, which were too big and which she had stuffed at the toes with rag. She had told nobody. She had left a note for Sefa at Orley's that said only *gone to look at something, back by the bell*, and she had not gone to the watch house, because she did not know what she would say to Tobin through a grille.

Kesh was late. Ilse stood on the last stone of the causeway with the wind coming in off the sea and watched the water go out. It went quickly on a spring ebb. You could hear it going, a hiss and a rustle in the dark, and you could see the mud come up out of it, shining under the cloudy moon, ridged and puddled and laced with channels where the last of the tide was running.

"You came," said Kesh, behind her.

Ilse did not jump this time. "You said I would."

"I said you'd want to. Wanting and coming aren't the same, in my experience." Kesh had a coil of rope over her shoulder and a shuttered lantern in her hand and was wearing, Ilse noticed, no boots at all. Her feet and shins were bare and grey with mud. "Boots are no good out there. The mud takes them. You'll see." She held out the end of the rope. "Tie that round your waist. If you go in past your knees, don't struggle. Lie flat and shout."

"Have you lost people out here?"

"Not yet," said Kesh, and stepped off the end of the causeway into the dark.

They walked for an hour. Ilse had lived beside the flats her whole life and had never been out on them further than a child goes for cockles, and she had not known how big they were, or how strange. There was no up or down. The mud and the sky were the same colour and the water in the channels reflected the sky, so that she seemed to be walking on a thin skin stretched over nothing. Twice she went in to the knee and Kesh hauled her out on the rope without a word. Once something moved in a channel beside them, large and slow, and Kesh stopped and shuttered the lantern and they stood in the dark until it had gone.

"Seal," said Kesh afterwards.

"Are you sure?"

"No."

The warehouses came up out of the dark one at a time. They were bigger than Ilse had thought, four storeys of black timber and brick, roofless, their windows empty, the high-water line drawn round them in weed at the height of a man's head. Doors hung from one hinge. A crane jutted out from the top of the nearest, its chain still hanging, and the wind made the chain swing and knock against the wall with a sound like someone patiently asking to be let in.

"Which one?" said Ilse.

"You tell me. You've got the plan."

Ilse unrolled her copy under the lantern. Her hands were cold and the paper kept curling. The culvert came off the edge of Hanne's drawing pointing east by a little south. She looked up and found the Exchange, a dark bulk against the faint lamplit haze of the town, and turned until it was behind her, and looked along the line.

"That one. The one with the crane."

"That's what I'd have said," said Kesh. "But I wanted to hear you say it."

scenes.title: Below the Weed Line
scenes.text:
Inside, the warehouse was a well of black. The upper floors had fallen in long ago and their beams lay heaped across the ground floor in a tangle, slimed with weed, and through the tangle the mud was littered with things the tide had brought: a cartwheel, a ship's bucket, a dead gull, a child's shoe. Kesh opened the lantern a crack and the light went up the walls and showed the weed line all round them, far above their heads.

"Spring tide comes in fast," said Kesh. "Faster than you'd think. We've got an hour and a half at the bottom of it. Maybe less. When I say go, we go, and we don't stop for anything. Agreed?"

"Agreed."

They found the culvert in the north-west corner, behind a fallen beam: a low brick arch at the bottom of the wall, half full of mud, with a trickle of black water running out of it. Someone had been there before them. The mud in front of the arch was trodden flat and there were marks in it, long straight drags, like something heavy being pulled, and beside the drags, very clear, the print of a boot.

And there were sacks.

They were stacked against the wall beside the culvert under an old sail, a dozen of them, maybe more, each stamped with a mark Ilse had seen a thousand times. The Harl mark. White salt. Kesh twitched back the edge of the sail and whistled through the gap in her teeth.

"There's your four sacks," she said. "And their brothers and sisters."

"They're bringing it in from the sea," said Ilse. "Not from the ships. Somebody's landing white salt out here, at the bottom of the tide, off the books, and carrying it up the culvert into cellar three. And then it's in the cellar book. And then it's real." She stared at the sacks. "Once it's in the cellar book, it's guild salt. Nobody can ever say it wasn't. It's been weighed and entered. It's been made honest."

"Clever," said Kesh. "Duty-free Harl white, laundered through the Exchange. You could sell that anywhere." She let the sail fall. "That's why they wanted your brother. A lighter can bring it right up the channel to the river side. It's too slow carrying it by hand through the mud."

"And when he said no, they burnt his boat and put him in the water beside it." Ilse's voice was shaking and she could not stop it. "So he'd be in a cell on Thursday and nobody would listen to him."

"Or so he'd be dead," said Kesh. "I don't think they cared which."

The lantern light moved over the mouth of the culvert. Something pale was lying in the water there, just inside the arch, where the black trickle ran out. Ilse thought it was a sack at first. Then she saw the hand.

It was Pell.

He was lying face down in six inches of water with his arms out in front of him as though he had been crawling out of the culvert when he stopped. He had been there some time. Ilse knew him by his coat, which was a weigher's coat with the guild badge on the shoulder, and by the ink on his right hand, the same ink that was on hers. She had seen that hand write a thousand twos.

She did not scream. She was proud of that, too, afterwards, though she was not proud of very much else about that night. She sat down in the mud because her legs would not hold her, and Kesh crouched beside her with the lantern and looked at Pell for a long time without saying anything.

"He was coming out," Kesh said at last. "Not going in. Look at his hands. He was crawling out."

"He came to Hanne," said Ilse. "Yesterday. He asked her if there were copies of the cellar books. He was frightened."

"He had reason." Kesh reached out, and hesitated, and then put her hand into the pocket of Pell's coat. When she drew it out she was holding a fold of oilcloth, tied with string. "He had this. I saw him with it, on the quay, last week. He was showing it to somebody. Arguing."

She untied the string. Inside the oilcloth was a letter.

The paper was good, heavy and cream, the kind that came from the stationers on the Mount where the council houses were. It had been folded three times and sealed, and the seal had been broken, and Ilse could see the half of it that remained: a ship, under full sail, in red wax.

"That's Corran's ring," said Kesh.

The letter was short. Ilse read it twice in the light of the lantern while the water ran past her knees.

*C.— The gate will be cleared by the eleventh. After that the culvert is yours at every spring ebb until the council votes. I will see that the vote does not come before the new year. The clerk is a concern. M. says he can manage her. If he cannot, I will. Burn this.*

It was not signed. But at the bottom, where a signature would be, there was a small mark in the same ink: two crossed keys inside a circle.

Ilse knew the mark. Every child in Varrow knew it. It was carved over the door of the council house, and printed on the council's bills, and embroidered in silver on the grey cloaks of the six councillors who sat for the town.

"The clerk," said Ilse. "That's me."

"That's you," Kesh agreed.

"And M. is Merrit Vael."

"Or any other M. in a town full of them." Kesh folded the letter back into its oilcloth. "But I'd not bet against it."

The water at Ilse's knees had grown deeper while she read. She noticed it all at once, the way you notice a sound only when it stops: the black trickle out of the culvert had become a stream, and the stream was flowing the wrong way. It was flowing *in*.

"Kesh."

"I see it." Kesh was already on her feet. "Go. Now."

scenes.title: The Crane
scenes.text:
They did not make it to the causeway.

They made it out of the warehouse door, and twenty yards across the mud, and then the channel they had crossed on the way in was not a channel any more but a river, waist-deep and racing, with the moon in it broken into a thousand pieces. Beyond it the next channel was filling, and beyond that the next. The flats were going under while they watched, not like water rising in a bath, but all at once and everywhere, the sea coming up out of the mud itself.

"Back," said Kesh. "Back inside. Up."

"Up where?"

Kesh pointed. The crane.

They climbed the inside of the warehouse wall by the beams that had fallen against it, and by the iron brackets that had once held the upper floors, and by Kesh's rope, which she threw over a bracket and hauled Ilse up on, twice, when her father's boots would not grip. Ilse lost one boot on the way up and did not go back for it. By the time they reached the top of the wall, where the crane's beam came out through a gap in the brickwork, the water was over the sacks of Harl white and swirling round the mouth of the culvert where Pell was, and still coming.

They sat on the crane beam with their backs to the wall, sixty feet above the flats, and watched the sea come in. It came in all night. It filled the warehouse to the weed line and then above it, and the chain of the crane swung below their feet with its end in the water. It was very cold. Kesh gave Ilse her coat and sat in her shirt with her arms round her knees and did not seem to feel it.

"Why are you doing this?" Ilse said, sometime in the hour before dawn, when she could no longer feel her feet and had stopped trying. "Really. Not for five crowns."

Kesh was quiet for so long that Ilse thought she had fallen asleep.

"I carried for Corran," she said at last. "In the summer. Before I knew what it was. Three loads, out here, at the bottom of the tide. He paid me well. And then he stopped paying me, and told me if I talked I'd end up like the last carrier he'd had." She looked down at the water. "I didn't know what he meant then. I thought he was just talking."

"And now you do."

"Now I do." Kesh wiped her face with the back of her hand. "Pell wasn't a bad man. He drank and he couldn't write a straight two. But he wasn't a bad man."

The sky over the sea went from black to grey to a thin, dirty white. The tide turned. Ilse felt it turn, somehow, though she could see nothing change: some pressure went off the air. Far off across the water, a bell was ringing in the town.

She counted the strokes, from habit. Six. The six o'clock bell. At the Exchange the porters would be sweeping and the tally desk would be empty.

And at the foot of Tarrant Stair, the watch would be getting Tobin ready to go before the magistrate.

scenes.title: The Councillor's House
scenes.text:
The tide let them go a little before noon.

They came down off the crane when the water had dropped below the weed line, and waded, and then walked, and then, for the last half mile, ran, Ilse in one boot and one stocking with the oilcloth packet buttoned inside Kesh's coat. At the end of the causeway Kesh stopped.

"This is where I leave you," she said.

"Come with me. To the watch. Tell Orrin what you saw."

"Orrin's watch has three men in it I've paid and one I'm paying now." Kesh pulled her coat off Ilse's shoulders, and Ilse felt the cold come in like a hand. "Keep the letter. You're a clerk. People believe clerks." She hesitated. "Pell. Somebody ought to go out and get him. Before the next tide takes him further in."

"I'll tell them."

"Don't tell them I was there." And Kesh was gone up Gull Street at a run, barefoot, her coat flapping, and two fishwives turned to watch her go and then turned to stare at Ilse, who was standing at the end of the causeway in the middle of the day covered in mud to the waist, with one boot.

She went to the watch house first. She did not think about it. Her feet took her.

Captain Orrin was not there. A sergeant with a cold told her that the magistrate had not sat that morning, on account of the *Gull* still lying across the channel and half the bench being shipowners who had business with the harbour; that the hearing had been put back to Friday; and that her brother was in good health, and had eaten his breakfast, and was not, at present, receiving visitors except by the captain's leave.

"Tell the captain," said Ilse, "that there's a dead man in the drowned warehouse on the east flats. The one with the crane. It's Gerrit Pell, the north quay weigher."

The sergeant looked at her mud, and at her one boot, and wrote it down very slowly.

Then she went home and washed and put on her other dress, the brown one, and her mother's good shawl, and sat on the edge of Tobin's cot with the letter in her lap and thought.

She could take it to the watch. But Kesh said the watch was bought, or some of it, and Orrin had looked at her too long in that cold room as though he could see the scrap of tally paper through her stays. She could take it to the guild. But the guild was Merrit Vael, and M. said he could manage her. She could take it to the magistrate on Friday, in open court, in front of half the bench who were shipowners with business with the harbour.

Or she could take it to the council.

Not the council. One councillor. The one who had asked Vael to look into the water gate in the first place — Hanne had said so — and who had been asking for years about the spring tides, every year the water a little higher. The one in the grey cloak who had been talking to Vael in the hall on Monday, and who, Ilse had thought at the time, had not looked as though she much liked what she was hearing.

Aud Brennick's house was on the Mount, at the top of the town, where the streets were wide and the houses had gardens and you could not smell the flats at all. A maid let her in. She was shown into a long room with a fire at each end and a carpet so thick that her feet made no sound on it, and asked to wait, and waited.

Councillor Brennick came in after a quarter of an hour. She was a handsome woman of fifty with iron-grey hair cut short and the kind of stillness that comes from never having had to hurry. She did not sit.

"Miss Marrow. My maid says you have something for the council."

Ilse held it out. "I found it on a dead man."

Brennick took the oilcloth and unfolded it and read the letter. She read it once. Her face did not change at all. Then she folded it again, along its old folds, and held it in both hands.

"Where?"

Ilse told her. She told her about the four sacks and the cellar book and the culvert and the warehouse and Pell. She did not tell her about Kesh. She did not tell her about the page she had cut out of the cellar book, which was still inside her stays, though she could not have said why she kept that back, except that her hand had gone to it, once, while she was talking, and she had taken it away again.

Brennick listened to the end.

"You've been very brave," she said, "and very foolish, and I think more the first than the second. Does anyone else know of this?"

"No one. My brother knows about the man on the south pans. That's all."

"And Master Vael?"

"He knows I saw the four sacks. He told me to write it up as Pell's mistake."

"Did he." Brennick turned and looked into the fire. "I have suspected for some months that something in the guild was not as it should be. I asked Master Vael to look into the water gate in the summer, and he told me there was nothing to look into. Now I see why." She turned back. "Leave this with me, Miss Marrow. I'll take it before the council tomorrow, in closed session. And I'll speak to the magistrate about your brother tonight. He'll not go before the bench on Friday. You have my word."

"Thank you."

"Go home. Speak to no one. If Master Vael asks you anything, you know nothing. Can you do that?"

"Yes."

The maid showed her out. On the way through the hall Ilse passed a writing table by the window, with a stand of pens and a dish of sand and a stack of paper on it, heavy and cream, and a stick of red sealing wax.

It meant nothing. Every house on the Mount bought its paper from the same stationer. Every councillor sealed in red.

She walked home very fast and did not look back once.

scenes.title: Visiting Hours
scenes.text:
The captain's leave, as it turned out, could be had for a basket.

Sefa brought bread, and a pot of Mistress Orley's fish stew with a cloth tied over it, and a clean shirt of Tobin's that she had taken off the line at Coil Lane, and a little jar of goose grease for his hand. She set them down on the table in front of the sergeant with the cold and smiled at him, and kept smiling, until he got up and unlocked the iron door.

Tobin was sitting on the bench in the cell with his back against the wall. His left hand was bound up in grey rag. He looked up when she came in and his whole face changed, and then changed again, carefully, into something else.

"Sefa."

"You owe me a shilling," said Sefa. She sat down on the bench beside him and put the basket on his knees. "Eat that. Mistress Orley made it and she'll ask."

He ate. He ate like a man who has had nothing but watch-house gruel for three days, which he had, and she watched him and did not say anything until the pot was empty.

"Where's Ilse?"

"Out. She left me a note last night. *Gone to look at something.*" Sefa took his bad hand and began to unwind the rag. "She came back at noon looking like something the tide brought in, and went to the watch, and then she went home and put her good shawl on and went up the Mount."

"The Mount? Who does she know on the Mount?"

"Nobody. That's what worries me." Sefa got the rag off. The burn ran across his palm and up the inside of his fingers, shiny and red. She opened the goose grease. "Hold still."

He held still. She worked the grease into the burn, gently, and he did not make a sound, though his jaw went tight.

"I saw her go out," Sefa said. "The *Gull*. I was on the roof at Orley's. Somebody was steering her. I told Ilse and I've told the captain."

"I know. He told me." Tobin looked at his hand. "Sefa. When I got to her, out at the bar. She was already burning. Nobody aboard. But there was a boat pulling away. A gig, four oars, going east, toward the drowned warehouses. I saw it against the fire. And there was a man in the stern of it, and he turned round to look at the *Gull*, and the light was on his face."

"Did you know him?"

"I didn't think so. Not then." Tobin was quiet. "But I've been sitting here three days with nothing to do but think, and I've been thinking about it. And I've seen him since. I've seen him in the Exchange. Talking to Master Vael by the clock, a week back, the day I came in for my pay. A big man, soft-spoken. Southern. With a ring."

"Corran," said Sefa.

Tobin stared at her. "How do you know that name?"

"Because there's a girl called Kesh who drinks at the Lantern and talks too much when she's had three, and she's been talking about a man called Corran since the summer." Sefa wound a clean strip of linen round his hand, firmly. "Half the rope walk knows that name, Tobin. We just don't know who it belongs to."

"Tell Ilse," Tobin said. "Tell her Vael knows him. Tell her tonight."

"I will."

"And Sefa." He caught her hand with his good one. "Tell her not to go up the Mount again."

scenes.title: Cellar Three
scenes.text:
The Exchange was closed when Ilse got there, but the side door was on the latch, and the lamp was lit in the tally room.

Merrit Vael was sitting at her desk.

He had the cellar book for cellar three open in front of him, at the ninth, at the place where the page had been. He had laid his hand flat over the stub, as though he could feel through his palm where it had gone.

"Sit down, Miss Marrow," he said.

She did not sit down.

"I've been master of this guild for eleven years," Vael said. He did not look up. "In that time I have never known a page to go missing from a cellar book. Not one. Not through damp, not through fire, not through the carelessness of a clerk. And the night after I tell you to write up the *Constant* as Pell's error, a page goes. The very page." He turned the book toward her. "I'm not angry. I want you to understand that. I'm frightened. Where is it?"

"Safe."

"Is it." He sat back. In the lamplight he looked older than she had ever seen him, and very tired. "Miss Marrow. I told you to write it up as forty-six because I have been watching the cellar book for cellar three since the first week of July, and I did not want whoever is writing those entries to know that anyone else had noticed. I have been building a case. A slow one. With care." He spread his hands. "And then Pell disappeared, and your brother's boat burned, and the case is no longer slow."

"Pell is dead," said Ilse.

Vael closed his eyes.

"Where?"

"In the culvert. At the warehouse end. I found him last night."

"With anything on him?"

She did not answer, and he opened his eyes and looked at her, and she saw him understand.

"You found a letter," he said. "Where is it?"

"I took it to the council."

"To the council."

"To Councillor Brennick."

For a moment Merrit Vael did not move at all. Then he stood up, so suddenly that the stool went over behind him, and the lamp jumped on the desk and the shadows jumped with it.

"Miss Marrow," he said, very quietly, "who do you suppose cleared the water gate?"

scenes.title: The River Door
scenes.text:
The wind got up while they were still in the tally room. Ilse heard it come over the roof of the Exchange in one long push, like a hand going over a cat, and the windows of the great hall rattled in their leads, and somewhere a shutter that nobody had fastened began to bang.

"Spring tide," said Vael. "And a westerly behind it. It'll come over the seawall tonight. It does, one year in five." He righted the stool and did not sit on it. "If you wanted to flood cellar three — if you wanted every sack in it wet and every book in this room ruined and the culvert full of mud for a twelvemonth — you would open the river door tonight, at the top of the flood, and let the sea do the rest."

"And no one would ever know how much salt had been in it."

"No one would ever know anything." He picked up the lamp. "Will you come and look? I would rather not go alone. I am fifty-eight years old and I have never in my life been brave."

They went down by the cellar stair. Cellar three was the oldest of the six, a long vault of black brick with the salt stacked along both walls in its sacks, white and grey, the white on pallets to keep it off the damp. The air tasted of it. At the far end, where the vault narrowed, there should have been a wall of newer, paler brick where the river door had been closed up when Ilse was a child.

There was not. There was an arch, and in the arch a pair of old oak gates, black with age and wet, and between the gates a gap the width of a man, and through the gap the sound of water.

"Cleared by the eleventh," said Ilse.

"The bricks came out in the summer. A course at a time. From the other side." Vael held up the lamp. "Look at the hinges. Someone's greased them."

On the floor in front of the gates the salt was trodden into a path, and the path led to the stacks of white, and there, between two pallets, were the four sacks of Harl white from the *Constant* that were not from the *Constant* at all. Ilse knew them by their stamp, which was a good stamp, but not quite right: the Harl ship on it had one mast too many.

"They forged the mark," she said.

"They forged everything. The mark, the entries, the weighing." Vael set the lamp down on a pallet. "All they needed was a clerk who would write what she was given. Pell was frightened into it. Mott the cellarman was paid. And you—"

"I wasn't."

"No," said Vael. "You weren't. That's why the letter calls you a concern."

The water beyond the gates was louder now. It came up the old slip in surges, with the wind behind each one, and each surge reached a little further across the stones before it slid back.

"We should go," said Ilse. "We should go to Orrin, now, with this—"

"Nobody's coming," said a voice behind them, and the lamp on the pallet swung its light round as somebody kicked it, and went out.

In the dark, a hand closed on Ilse's arm, hard, and she heard Vael cry out, and heard him fall. Then there was another light, a bull's-eye lantern, opened full in her face, and behind it a big soft-spoken shape that said, quite gently, "Don't scream, Miss Marrow. There's nobody in the building to hear."

"Corran," she said.

"If you like." The light moved off her face and she saw him. He was large and fair and tired-looking, a man you would pass in the street, with a heavy southern coat and, on the hand that held the lantern, a ring with a ship on it. "I'm sorry about your brother's boat. That wasn't my idea."

"Whose was it?"

He did not answer. Behind him, coming down the cellar stair with a lamp of her own, her grey cloak held up off the wet stones, was Councillor Brennick.

"Mine," she said. "I'm afraid it was. Hello, Merrit."

Vael was on the floor by the pallets, holding his head. He looked up at her.

"Aud," he said. "I did think it might be you. I hoped I was wrong."

"You always hope that. It's why you've never been any use." Brennick came down the last step and looked around the vault, at the salt, at the gates, at the water sliding in under them. "The clerk had the page from the cellar book, Corran. She didn't give it to me. I watched her hand go to it. It's in her bodice."

Corran held out his hand.

Ilse thought about not giving it. She thought about it very hard, standing in the dark in cellar three with the sea coming in under the river door. And then she thought about Pell face down in the culvert, and took the page out of her stays and held it out, and when Corran reached for it she let it go a moment early, so that it fell between them into the water on the floor.

He bent to catch it.

The next surge came in through the gates with a sound like a door slamming, and it was not like the others. It came up to Ilse's knees and over the pallets and knocked Corran off his feet and took his lantern and drowned it, and in the black that followed Ilse heard Brennick shout, and heard the oak gates groan back on their greased hinges as the sea opened them wide.

scenes.title: Over the Seawall
scenes.text:
She did not remember, afterwards, finding the stair. She remembered the water, which was so cold it did not feel like water but like being struck all over at once, and the salt in it, which got in her mouth and her eyes and seemed to be inside her chest. She remembered Vael's hand finding her sleeve. She remembered the sacks of white salt going past her in the dark, turning over in the current, melting.

And she remembered a light at the top of the cellar stair, and a voice she knew shouting her name, and then Tobin's hand, his good hand, closing on her wrist and pulling.

They came up into the great hall of the Exchange. The windows on the west side had gone and the wind was in the hall, and the rain with it, and the floor was an inch deep in water that had come over the seawall and down Quay Street and in under the doors. Somebody had lit the gas under the great clock. In its light Ilse saw Tobin, soaked and furious, with his bound hand held up against his chest; and Sefa behind him, with a boathook; and Captain Orrin, in his blue coat, with four of the watch.

"How," said Ilse. "How did you—"

"Sefa came to the watch house," said Orrin, "with a pot of stew and a story about Master Vael and a man called Corran. I didn't believe the stew or the story. But your brother did, and he was making a great deal of noise about it, and I thought I'd rather have him where I could see him." He looked past her down the stair. "Who's down there?"

"Brennick," said Vael, behind her. He was sitting on the bottom step, holding his head. There was blood in his beard. "And Corran, whatever his name is. And Mott, I expect, somewhere. And the river."

Orrin looked at him for a moment. Then he turned to his men.

"Ropes," he said. "And lanterns. We're going down."

They brought up Corran first, half drowned and cursing, with his ring hand broken where the gate had caught it. Then Mott the cellarman, who had been hiding behind the stacks of grey and who came up weeping and talking before anyone had asked him anything. Brennick they found last, at the top of the old slip, beyond the gates, clinging to the iron winch that had stood there for a hundred years waiting for barges that never came. She had lost her cloak. She did not say anything at all when they brought her up, and did not look at anyone, and when Orrin put the irons on her she held out her wrists as though she were accepting a glass of wine.

At the top of the stair she stopped beside Ilse.

"The letter's ash," she said. "And the page is in the sea. You'll find it hard to prove anything, Miss Marrow."

"I'm a clerk," said Ilse. "I wrote it all down."

scenes.title: The Tally Desk
scenes.text:
They pulled the *Gull* off the bar on the next ebb. There was not much left of her. Tobin stood on the north quay and watched the salvage men bring her in, a black spine with a few ribs, and said nothing for a long time, and then said that she had been a good old boat and that he supposed he would have to learn to fish from the shore.

Pell they brought in on the same tide. His wife came to the quay and stood beside the cart with her hands folded and did not cry, and Ilse went and stood with her, and neither of them said anything, and it seemed to be what was wanted.

The magistrate sat on the following Tuesday. He heard Orrin, and Vael, and Mott, who talked for an hour and a half and could not be stopped, and the sergeant with the cold, and finally Ilse. She had brought her own ledger: a small book with a marbled cover, in which, every night since the night of the north quay, she had written down everything she had seen and when. The four sacks. The cellar book entries, copied out week by week, back to midsummer. The culvert. The letter, word for word, with the mark of the crossed keys drawn at the bottom as carefully as she could draw it. The magistrate read it through twice, and asked her whether she had written it at the time or afterward, and she told him at the time, every night, and showed him where the ink changed when her pen had needed cutting.

Tobin was discharged without a stain. Corran's real name turned out to be Anselm Rook, a factor of the Harl salt houses, wanted in two other ports. Councillor Brennick was held for the assize.

Kesh did not come to the hearing. But on the morning after it, when Ilse came into the Exchange at six with her sleeves already pinned, there was a pair of sea boots standing on the tally desk, her father's, the one she had lost on the crane wall and the one she had not, and stuffed into the toe of the first was a scrap of paper that said, in a sprawling hand, *you owe me five crowns.*

Sefa came at noon with bread.

"Your counting face," she said, sitting on the step below the desk, which was still not allowed. "The old one. The good one."

"Is it?"

"It is." Sefa tore the loaf. "What are you counting?"

Ilse showed her. It was the cellar book for cellar three, dried out page by page in front of the fire in the tally room, cockled and stained and smelling of the sea. At the ninth, where the stub of the cut page was, she had pasted in a fresh leaf. On it, in her own hand, she had written the entry for the *Constant* as it should have been.

Forty-two sacks of Harl white. Received at the north quay. Weighed. Entered.

And underneath, smaller, in the margin, where a clerk notes a correction:

*Four sacks struck. See the magistrate's record. — I. M.*

"There," said Ilse. "Now it adds."
